newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bomb judge to allow victims at trial.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bomb judge to allow victims at trial.

text.p: The judge in the Oklahoma City bombing case reversed himself Tuesday, agreeing to allow victims of the bombing to attend the trial even if they plan to testify in the death penalty phase of the case.

U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch said he took into consideration a law signed last week by President Clinton that prohibited federal judges from excluding victims who may testify about the impact of a crime on them or their families.

The trial of Timothy McVeigh is scheduled to begin in Denver on March 31. "A debate now on the constitutionality of this new legislation would result in a delay of that trial," the judge wrote in a five-page decision.

He said he could protect McVeigh's right to a fair trial by questioning the victims outside the presence of the jury before they testified to determine if they were unduly influenced by what they heard or saw.

Until the law took effect, federal court rules barred potential witnesses from attending court proceedings before they testified in order to prevent their testimony being influenced by what they heard. Matsch had extended that rule last year, saying victims who attended the trial could not even testify in the penalty phase of the trial, assuming a conviction.

Some of the victims said they were angry about the judge's decision and mounted a campaign against it. They first appealed unsuccessfully and then turned to Congress, which quickly passed the new law, which Clinton signed.
The victims were already disappointed that the trial was moved to Denver, making it difficult for many of them to attend.
Since the law was signed, some of the victims and a national victim organisation, the National Organisation for Victim Assistance, asked Matsch to hold a hearing on its application.

He cautioned in his written order that victim impact testimony was the "most problematical of the aggravating factors" that jurors would consider in deciding whether the defendants were executed. The prosecution has asked for the death penalty.
A special closed-circuit telecast for victims was mandated by Congress last year. The new law also allows victims who plan to testify to attend the closed-circuit telecast.

"All interests, including the public interest in proceeding with Mr McVeigh's trial, can be accommodated by construing (the new law) as simply reversing the presumption of a prejudicial effect ..." the judge wrote.
McVeigh and former Army buddy Terry Nichols are charged with the bombing. Nichols will be tried at a later date.
